no_intervention_scenario.summary: Over the next 5 to 10 years without deliberate intervention, physical tape decay, broadcaster insolvency, urban-centric media homogenization, and unconsented commercial voice scraping will hollow out regional and generational Lebanese spoken varieties while privatizing whatever digitized speech remains.
what_is_lost: Magnetic U-matic, Betacam, and reel-to-reel archives at public and private Lebanese broadcasters suffer irreversible binder hydrolysis and vinegar syndrome before rights disputes are resolved.
Distinct rural, mountain, Bekaa, northern, and southern micro-lexicons, prosodic contours, and occupational idioms collapse into a flattened Levantine-Beiruti media register.
Unscripted elder speech, oral poetry (zajal), and non-literate storytelling traditions vanish as older speakers pass away without intergenerational transmission mechanisms.
Publicly posted Lebanese voice clips on social platforms are scraped into proprietary commercial datasets, stripping local communities of attribution, governance, and economic return.
what_value_remains: Intact everyday vernacular vitality in informal family networks, local markets, religious gatherings, and diaspora households where spoken Lebanese remains the primary medium of intimacy and humor.
Rich private family cassette, VHS, and smartphone voice-note collections held across Lebanon and the global diaspora.
Existing broadcaster master vaults, including Télé Liban's foundational audiovisual holdings, which retain high cultural value if rescued before physical failure.
Living oral performers, folk poets, craftspeople, and elders who still carry specialized registers and collective memory.

support.claim: Télé Liban holds foundational audiovisual archives dating back to 1959 that represent major national social and cultural history.
support.fragment: Founded in 1959 as the first public television station in the Arab world, Télé Liban preserves major audiovisual archives

support.claim: Unmaintained magnetic media in hot, humid, or power-unstable storage environments degrades chemically within years, making legal clearance moot if physical carriers fail first.
premises: Analog videotape and audiotape bases degrade through moisture absorption and chemical breakdown.
Chronic power outages and underfunded climate control in Lebanon accelerate storage instability.
Rights clearance for legacy broadcasts often takes years due to fragmented contracts.

support.claim: Spoken heritage has intrinsic civic and identity value to Lebanese communities regardless of its utility for commercial speech technologies.

faces_found.what_it_requires: Compliance with Literary and Artistic Property Protection Law No. 75/1999 and Electronic Transactions and Personal Data Law No. 81/2018, which lack explicit text-and-data-mining exceptions, orphan-work safe harbors, or tailored cultural heritage archival exemptions.

faces_found.face: EU data protection (GDPR) imposed by foreign funders
faces_found.what_it_requires: Lawful basis, explicit informed consent or strict public-interest archival safeguards, data minimization, cross-border transfer rules, and right-to-erasure workflows for identifiable voice recordings.

faces_found.face: Real market practice of commercial web harvesting
faces_found.what_it_requires: Technical, contractual, and access-tier defenses against automated scraping of public audio/video repositories by commercial technology firms harvesting voice data without consent or compensation.

faces_found.face: Copyright and broadcaster ownership of archives
faces_found.what_it_requires: Navigating overlapping neighboring rights of broadcasters, scriptwriters, composers, performers, and interviewees across state-owned and private bankrupt or restructured stations.

faces_found.face: Physical carrier obsolescence and infrastructure precarity
faces_found.what_it_requires: Working playback decks, spare parts, stable electricity, and climate-controlled cold storage before analog tapes become unreadable.

faces_found.face: Diglossia and urban linguistic prestige bias
faces_found.what_it_requires: Counteracting institutional habits that treat Modern Standard Arabic or elite Beiruti speech as worthy of preservation while dismissing rural, Bedouin, Armenian-Lebanese, or working-class accents as 'uneducated'.

faces_found.face: Oral community norms and non-literate consent
faces_found.what_it_requires: Audio-recorded verbal consent protocols, family/village stewardship agreements, and honor-based attribution rather than inaccessible written legal forms.

options.name: Broadcaster Dark-Archive Escrow and Orphan-Work Safe Harbor
options.description: Establish an independent national custodial trust that physically digitizes deteriorating radio and television tapes from public and private stations under sealed escrow before commercial rights are fully cleared. Broadcasters retain commercial exploitation rights while the trust gains statutory or contractual permission for preservation copying and non-commercial research access.
who_benefits: Future generations
Researchers and educators
Cash-strapped broadcasters whose tapes are decaying
who_could_be_left_out: Non-literate citizens if access portals require academic credentials
Informal local community voices never recorded by mainstream stations
faces_affected: Copyright and broadcaster ownership of archives
Lebanese statutory law as written
Physical carrier obsolescence and infrastructure precarity
options.what_would_make_it_fail: Broadcasters refusing physical handover due to fear of losing control over monetizable political or entertainment footage.

support.claim: Lebanon's intellectual property and personal data rules are governed by separate statutes that require structured legal accommodation for digital media.
support.fragment: Literary and Artistic Property Protection Law No. 75 dated 4/3/1999. Electronic Transactions and Personal Data Law No. 81 dated 1/10/2018.

support.claim: Separating physical preservation from commercial licensing prevents tape decay while rights disputes remain unresolved.
premises: Digitization for preservation does not inherently require immediate public broadcast.
Escrow agreements reassure rights holders that commercial release remains gated.

options.name: Municipal Library Cassette and VHS Rescue Kiosks
options.description: Equip municipal cultural centers, public libraries, and school hubs across rural districts with rugged, offline tape-to-digital transfer stations staffed by trained youth. Residents bring family weddings, village festivals, and elder interviews on cassette or VHS, receiving a free digital copy while optionally donating a copy under spoken-consent tiers.
who_benefits: Rural and regional communities
Low-income families without digitization equipment
Older people holding home media
who_could_be_left_out: Diaspora households abroad without local drop-off access
Families distrustful of municipal authorities
faces_affected: Physical carrier obsolescence and infrastructure precarity
Oral community norms and non-literate consent
EU data protection (GDPR) imposed by foreign funders
options.what_would_make_it_fail: Unreliable electricity at municipal centers or families fearing private domestic footage will leak online.

support.claim: Decentralized regional transfer stations capture vernacular speech excluded from Beirut-based broadcast archives.
premises: Commercial broadcasters disproportionately recorded urban and elite speech.
Home cassettes hold authentic local dialects and everyday conversation.
Free local transfer removes economic barriers for low-income households.

options.name: Kaitiakitanga-Style Sovereign Lebanese Voice Data License
options.description: Adapt the Māori Kaitiakitanga guardianship license model into a bespoke Lebanese custodial license governing any digitized broadcast or community speech corpus. The license prohibits commercial harvesting, resale, or model training without explicit community governance approval and benefit-sharing, while permitting free educational and cultural use.
who_benefits: All Lebanese speech communities
Diaspora educators
Local creators protected from uncompensated scraping
who_could_be_left_out: Users outside formal institutions if enforcement relies solely on courtroom litigation
faces_affected: Real market practice of commercial web harvesting
Copyright and broadcaster ownership of archives
Lebanese statutory law as written
options.what_would_make_it_fail: Large commercial scrapers ignoring contractual terms unless paired with gated streaming and watermarking.

support.claim: Indigenous speech stewards have developed guardianship licenses where data is cared for under community sovereignty rather than surrendered to open scraping.
support.fragment: A licence developed by Te Hiku Media under which data is not owned but cared

support.claim: Cultural voice archives should be governed as a guarded commons rather than surrendered to extractive open-web licensing.

options.name: Acoustic-First Voice Archive for Non-Literate Users
options.description: Design the entire discovery, consent, cataloging, and playback experience around spoken audio prompts, voice navigation, and iconographic maps rather than written Arabic or Latin text. Elders and non-literate speakers browse recordings by tapping village landmarks, occupations, or seasonal themes and record spoken tags in their own dialect.
who_benefits: People who do not read or write
Older people with visual or literacy barriers
Dialect speakers whose vocabulary lacks standardized spelling
who_could_be_left_out: Users on ultra-basic 2G feature phones without smartphone or kiosk access
Deaf and hard-of-hearing users unless paired with visual sign/text layers
faces_affected: Oral community norms and non-literate consent
Diglossia and urban linguistic prestige bias
options.what_would_make_it_fail: Off-the-shelf speech recognition failing on rural Lebanese phonology, frustrating non-literate users.

support.claim: Text-dependent metadata systems structurally exclude non-literate speakers from describing and retrieving their own oral heritage.
premises: Lebanese Arabic has no single standardized orthography.
Requiring typed metadata privileges educated urban catalogers over native rural speakers.

options.name: Diaspora-to-Village Voice-Note Oral History Circles
options.description: Run structured, low-bandwidth asynchronous audio exchange circles over encrypted messaging apps connecting diaspora grandchildren with grandparents in Lebanese villages. Weekly spoken prompts trigger story recordings about local proverbs, recipes, and place names, which are archived with spoken consent in family and village collections.
who_benefits: Diaspora youth losing fluency
Older people experiencing isolation
Household-level lineages
who_could_be_left_out: Families without diaspora ties or reliable mobile data
Public researchers if families keep circles strictly private
faces_affected: EU data protection (GDPR) imposed by foreign funders
Oral community norms and non-literate consent
options.what_would_make_it_fail: Platform lock-in on proprietary messaging apps where exported audio loses context or gets deleted when phones break.

support.claim: Everyday messaging voice notes already serve as Lebanon's largest living spoken-language medium across borders.
premises: Voice notes require zero literacy and work on low-cost smartphones.
Intergenerational family curiosity creates intrinsic motivation without external subsidies.

options.name: Hyper-Local Dialect Community Radio Network
options.description: Inspired by Ireland's Raidió na Gaeltachta, establish low-power regional FM and internet radio blocks dedicated exclusively to unscripted local speech, storytelling, call-in debates, and folk music in regional Lebanese dialects without switching to Modern Standard Arabic or Beiruti media norms.
who_benefits: Rural and regional communities
Older people and non-literate listeners
Low-income households using inexpensive FM radios
who_could_be_left_out: Urban audiences unfamiliar with dense rural idioms unless contextualized
faces_affected: Diglossia and urban linguistic prestige bias
Lebanese statutory law as written
options.what_would_make_it_fail: Broadcast licensing bottlenecks under Lebanese audiovisual media laws or advertiser pressure to standardize speech.

support.claim: Dedicated vernacular broadcasting sustains living spoken registers by validating regional speech on air.
support.fragment: Raidió na Gaeltachta is Ireland's Irish language radio service, broadcasting exclusively in Irish.

support.claim: FM radio reaches non-literate, low-income, and elderly residents without requiring internet connectivity.
premises: FM receivers are low-cost and battery-operable during power cuts.
Hearing one's own village accent on broadcast radio reverses linguistic stigma.

options.name: Premise-Inversion Audit of Live Vernacular Vitality
options.description: Before launching costly rescue drives, commission sociolinguistic field mapping across markets, TikTok/YouTube creators, gaming lobbies, and rural schools to test where spoken Lebanese is actually thriving or evolving rather than dying. Redirect preservation funds strictly toward documented endangered registers (e.g., disappearing artisanal trades, elderly village speech) instead of already-vibrant urban slang.
who_benefits: Truly endangered micro-dialects that would otherwise be drowned out
Funders avoiding wasted spend on self-sustaining urban speech
who_could_be_left_out: Hidden domestic registers not visible in public spaces or social media
faces_affected: Diglossia and urban linguistic prestige bias
Real market practice of commercial web harvesting
options.what_would_make_it_fail: Over-relying on online social media metrics, which falsely suggest vitality while masking offline rural language shift.

support.claim: Assuming uniform loss across all registers misallocates scarce preservation resources.
premises: Urban Lebanese is heavily represented on digital entertainment platforms.
Specialized rural, agricultural, and minority communal registers lack commercial media presence.

options.name: Live Zajal and Folk-Poetry Apprenticeship Stipends
options.description: Fund paid master-apprentice pairings between elder zajal poets, hakawati storytellers, and lament singers and young performers in regional towns, culminating in live public performances. Transmission happens embodied and face-to-face without requiring digital platforms or AI.
who_benefits: Older oral artists gaining income and recognition
Youth in low-income regions learning live rhetorical craft
Local audiences
who_could_be_left_out: Diaspora communities unable to attend live regional gatherings
faces_affected: Diglossia and urban linguistic prestige bias
Oral community norms and non-literate consent
options.what_would_make_it_fail: Short-term 6-month grant cycles ending before apprentices master improvisational meter and vocabulary.

support.claim: Improvisational oral genres survive through active performance ecosystems rather than passive archival storage.
premises: Zajal relies on real-time audience call-and-response and tonal wit.
Archiving recordings without living practitioners turns a living art into a museum artifact.

options.name: Broadcaster Archive Audio-Fingerprint and Watermark Shield
options.description: Embed imperceptible acoustic watermarks and deploy stream-only low-bitrate players with rate-limiting when broadcasters or heritage portals publish digitized Lebanese radio/TV clips online. This allows public listening by citizens and diaspora while deterring bulk automated harvesting by commercial speech-model scrapers.
who_benefits: Broadcasters worried about losing IP value
Community speakers protected from unauthorized voice cloning
Public listeners
who_could_be_left_out: Offline rural users and educators needing downloadable classroom files
faces_affected: Real market practice of commercial web harvesting
Copyright and broadcaster ownership of archives
options.what_would_make_it_fail: Overly restrictive DRM breaking playback on older smartphones or slow rural internet connections.

support.claim: Broadcasters withhold archives from public access largely because open web audio is immediately scraped by commercial actors.
premises: Unprotected audio URLs can be downloaded at scale in hours.
Technical friction and provenance watermarks reduce broadcaster reluctance to open archives.

options.name: Occupational Soundscapes and Craft Lexicon Field Recording
options.description: Deploy mobile recording teams to document disappearing workplace speech—stone masons, silk weavers, olive pressers, fishermen, and traditional bakers—capturing tool names, calls, bargaining idioms, and workplace humor on site.
who_benefits: Working-class and non-literate craftspeople
Future generations learning material culture
Linguists studying technical vernaculars
who_could_be_left_out: Domestic and unpaid care-work speech inside households
faces_affected: Diglossia and urban linguistic prestige bias
Oral community norms and non-literate consent
options.what_would_make_it_fail: Recording staged interviews instead of natural multi-speaker work interactions.

support.claim: Technical and artisanal vocabulary disappears fastest when traditional industries mechanize or close.
premises: Broadcast media rarely covers manual trades in authentic detail.
Lexical items tied to physical tools vanish once the tools leave daily use.

options.name: GDPR-Compliant Federated Local Data Residency Pods
options.description: Keep raw identifiable voice recordings and spoken consent records stored on encrypted servers physically or legally governed in Lebanon under community trusteeship, while exposing only anonymized, consent-verified metadata or aggregated linguistic features to EU-funded international partners.
who_benefits: Speakers whose biometric voice data stays under local control
Local projects needing foreign grants without surrendering raw data
who_could_be_left_out: Grassroots groups lacking technical staff to maintain federated infrastructure
faces_affected: EU data protection (GDPR) imposed by foreign funders
Lebanese statutory law as written
Real market practice of commercial web harvesting
options.what_would_make_it_fail: Power and connectivity outages in Lebanon making locally hosted pods unreachable without resilient solar-backed mirror nodes.

support.claim: Separating raw voice custody from external research access resolves conflicts between foreign funder privacy rules and local data sovereignty.
premises: GDPR imposes strict requirements on cross-border transfers of identifiable biometric voice data.
Federated access allows verification and scholarship without exporting raw files.

options.name: Dialect-Aware Automatic Alignment of Legacy Broadcasts
options.description: Use speech-to-text and speaker-diarization models fine-tuned on regional Lebanese phonology solely as an internal indexing assistant to generate searchable time-coded transcripts and phonetic tags for thousands of hours of uncataloged radio/TV tapes, reviewed by human dialect speakers.
who_benefits: Researchers, journalists, and educators searching vast unindexed tapes
Broadcasters unlocking buried cultural programming
who_could_be_left_out: Speakers of minority dialects if models hallucinate standard spellings and erase regional pronunciation
faces_affected: Copyright and broadcaster ownership of archives
Diglossia and urban linguistic prestige bias
options.what_would_make_it_fail: Treating noisy automated transcripts as authoritative text and discarding original audio nuances.

support.claim: Manual transcription of decades of broadcast tapes is prohibitively slow without automated first-pass indexing.
premises: Broadcasters hold tens of thousands of uncataloged audio-visual hours.

options.name: Household Kitchen-Table Proverb and Recipe Decks
options.description: Publish illustrated, phonetically intuitive card decks and audio-QR booklets of hyper-local proverbs, lullabies, curses, and seasonal food idioms collected within extended families, designed for dinner-table games across generations in Lebanon and the diaspora.
who_benefits: Children in Lebanon and diaspora households
Older family members positioned as household authorities
who_could_be_left_out: Non-literate adults if cards rely heavily on reading rather than audio playback
faces_affected: Diglossia and urban linguistic prestige bias
Oral community norms and non-literate consent

support.claim: Playful domestic artifacts trigger spontaneous spoken use inside families far more reliably than formal curricula.
premises: Proverbs and food idioms naturally surface during shared meals.
Physical decks work without electricity or internet access.

options.description: Create a collective licensing clearinghouse that charges commercial media producers, filmmakers, and vetted language-technology licensees a usage fee for authenticated Lebanese archival and community speech, routing micro-royalties back to surviving performers, rural contributors, and broadcaster preservation funds.
who_benefits: Low-income contributors and elders receiving direct income
Broadcasters gaining a self-financing preservation revenue stream
who_could_be_left_out: Contributors without bank accounts or formal ID if payment rails require formal banking
faces_affected: Copyright and broadcaster ownership of archives
Lebanese statutory law as written
Real market practice of commercial web harvesting

Older people and non-literate community elders
Low-income public school communities

faces_affected: Diglossia and urban linguistic prestige bias
Oral community norms and non-literate consent

options.description: Deploy rugged, solar-charged offline media servers with physical buttons and loudspeakers in village squares, clinics, and agricultural cooperatives, preloaded with regional folk tales, archival radio dramas, and oral histories accessible via local Wi-Fi or shared listening without internet.

People who do not read or write
Rural communities facing power and telecom outages

faces_affected: Physical carrier obsolescence and infrastructure precarity
Real market practice of commercial web harvesting

options.description: Build a public web and mobile acoustic map where users tap villages across Lebanon to hear parallel recordings of identical everyday sentences, folk terms, and vowel shifts spoken by different generations, visualizing how pronunciation and vocabulary shift across valleys and eras.

Regional speakers seeing their village represented

Villages with small populations omitted due to sparse sampling

options.name: Acoustic Restoration of Damaged Magnetic Broadcast Tapes
options.description: Apply specialized audio-restoration signal processing to remove wow-and-flutter, tape hiss, hum, and print-through from degraded radio dramas, political speeches, and folk broadcasts, preserving both the raw archival master and a clean listening master.
who_benefits: Older listeners with hearing loss needing clear speech intelligibility
Future generations accessing otherwise unintelligible recordings
who_could_be_left_out: Phonetic researchers if aggressive noise reduction alters fricatives and glottal stops and raw masters are not kept
faces_affected: Physical carrier obsolescence and infrastructure precarity
Copyright and broadcaster ownership of archives

support.claim: Degraded legacy recordings remain unusable for public transmission unless intelligibility is restored while retaining unedited masters.
premises: Decades-old broadcast tapes often suffer speed drift and heavy noise.
Dual-file archiving (raw master plus restored listening copy) protects both linguistic fidelity and public usability.
